title: Playbooks and roles
description: Write a playbook with several plays, scaffold its roles, then wire everything together with ansible.cfg and a site playbook.
outcomes: Target inventory groups with plays and order the roles they run
Use tags and role conditions to control what runs
Tell a role skeleton from the common role
Wire a project with ansible.cfg, roles_path and a site playbook

steps.intro: Playbooks decide what happens on which servers. Before we write one, we need servers in groups, so let's set up a small inventory quickly.
steps.inventoryName: Name it. The file becomes this name plus inventory.ini, and we'll point ansible.cfg at it later.
steps.import: Instead of typing every host, import an inventory you already have.
steps.paste: Here are three servers in two groups: web and db. In a real project you'd paste your own file.
steps.apply: kikx reads the hosts and the groups they belong to.
steps.saveInventory: Add it to the project. The web and db groups now exist, and playbooks can target them.
steps.configure: Playbooks and roles live in the Configure stage. Pick Playbook.
steps.playbookName: The name becomes the file name, here app.yml.
steps.folder: Many teams keep playbooks in a folder. Remember this: it changes where Ansible looks for roles, and we'll fix that at the end.
steps.play: A playbook is a list of plays. Each play answers two questions: which hosts, and which roles run on them.
steps.playName: Give the play a name that says what it does. It shows in the Ansible output as the play runs.
steps.allHosts: all is a special group that every host belongs to. Basics every server needs go here.
steps.commonRole: Then the roles, typed one by one with Enter. This play runs the common role.
steps.tags: Tags let you run part of a playbook later. Asking Ansible for the base tag runs only this play and skips the rest.
steps.addPlay: One file can hold several plays. Add a second one, for the web servers only.
steps.webHosts: This play targets the web group, so db1 is left alone.
steps.nginx: Its first role installs the web server.
steps.yourRole: The web servers also need certificates. Add the certbot role to the Web tier play, after nginx.
steps.roleOrder: The numbers show the order. Inside a play, roles run left to right, so nginx is ready before certbot asks it for a certificate.
steps.conditions: Not every role must always run. Role conditions add a when to a single role.
steps.when: certbot now runs only when enable_tls is true. Without the variable, the default filter keeps it off instead of failing.
steps.whenPreview: Look at the preview: certbot became a role with its own when line, while nginx stays a plain name.
steps.yourPlay: Add a third play named Database that runs the postgresql role on the db group.
steps.targeting: Each play's hosts line is its target: Prepare every host runs on all three servers, Web tier only on web1 and web2, Database only on db1.
steps.runOrder: Plays run top to bottom, and each finishes on all its hosts before the next starts: every server is prepared before the web tier is touched.
steps.savePlaybook: Add the playbook to the project.
steps.role: The playbook names roles, but they don't exist yet. A role skeleton creates one.
steps.roleName: The name must match the name used in the play exactly, or Ansible won't find it.
steps.skeleton: A skeleton is an empty but valid role: tasks, defaults, handlers and meta. It runs straight away, then you replace the placeholder task with your own.
steps.more: The less common entries hide behind Show more, to keep the list short. The common role is one of them.
steps.commonName: Name it common, the name our first play uses.
steps.commonPreview: Unlike a skeleton, it has settings, like the timezone every server gets, and real tasks: base packages, timezone, swap and a login message.
steps.difference: So a skeleton is an empty shape you fill in for your own app, while the common role is ready baseline setup for every server. That's why it runs on all.
steps.cfg: Last piece: tell Ansible where things are, with Ansible config, another entry Show more revealed.
steps.cfgInventory: Point it at our inventory file, so you don't need the inventory option on every command.
steps.rolesPath: Remember the folder? Ansible looks for roles next to the playbook, in playbooks/roles, which doesn't exist. roles_path points it at the roles folder at the root.
steps.cfgPreview: Two lines in ansible.cfg. Run Ansible from the folder that holds this file: it's read from the current directory.
steps.site: Finally, one entry point for everything: the site playbook.
steps.siteName: Call it site, so the whole project runs with ansible-playbook site.yml.
steps.siteImport: kikx lists the playbooks in this project. Import ours.
steps.importLine: Each import runs a whole playbook, in the order listed, so adding a playbook later is one more line here.
steps.checks: Checks reviews the result. It notices roles the playbook uses that no skeleton creates yet, and can scaffold them for you in one click.
steps.done: You built plays that target groups, ordered and conditioned roles, scaffolded roles and wired it all with ansible.cfg and site.yml. Look around, then try a playbook of your own.

checks.certbot: certbot is in the Web tier play
checks.name: A third play named Database

recap: A play pairs hosts with roles; a playbook runs its plays top to bottom.
Roles in a play run in the order listed; tags and when conditions narrow what runs.
A role skeleton is an empty role to fill in; the common role ships ready baseline tasks.
ansible.cfg points Ansible at the inventory and, through roles_path, at the roles folder.
site.yml imports every playbook, so one command runs the whole project.

demo.inventory:
[web]
web1 ansible_host=10.0.0.11
web2 ansible_host=10.0.0.12

[db]
db1 ansible_host=10.0.0.21
